sources.title: Tan Kah Kee (Q709049), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Tan Kah Kee', description 'Chinese businessman (1874-1961)', Chinese label 陈嘉庚, instance of human, born 21 October 1874, died 12 August 1961, citizenship Singapore, Malaysia and the Republic of China; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Heritage Board of Singapore, 'Tan Kah Kee: Adventurous merchant, legendary community leader', Roots.gov.sg (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: left Fujian for Singapore at 16 and rose in his father's rice business; when his father's businesses faltered he worked to wind them up and clear the debts, then built his own empire from a single pineapple cannery (three by the mid-1900s) into rubber, rice milling, a biscuit factory, shipping and the manufacture of tyres and shoes, branching into new markets when setbacks came; says his success was attributed to a fastidious nature and involvement in every stage of the supply chain (Henry Ford comparison), that he mentored Lee Kong Chian and Tan Lark Sye, that the businesses wound up through the Depression (the historian Wang Gungwu calls him one of the earliest global Chinese entrepreneurs), and that he helped found more than ten schools in Singapore including Tao Nan, Ai Tong and the Chinese High School and pushed for Xiamen University. Also covers wartime relief work, a postwar newspaper and British concern about him, which are not scored here. Government heritage story, admiring; its notes cite NLB biographies and a ThinkChina article. Its opening line says he set up 100 institutions while its body says more than ten schools, so no count is carded.

Arnold Wright and H. A. Cartwright (eds.), Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya: Its History, People, Commerce, Industries, and Resources (London: Lloyd's Greater Britain Publishing Company, 1908), Cornell University Library scan on the Internet Archive; the entry 'Tan Kah Kee' (p. 712, read in the OCR text) and the plate 'Business Men of Singapore'. Contemporary trade-directory profile written when he was 33: a rice merchant trading as Kiam Eik, native of Amoy and son of Tan Kee Peck, who entered his father's firm, began business on his own account fifteen years later and by 1908 conducted three pineapple-preserving factories supplied from his own 600-acre plantation, owned a 400-acre estate of Para rubber one year old, traded in rice and sugar with Hong Kong and Shanghai, and belonged to the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. Subscription-style commercial publication, flattering by genre; says nothing of schools or philanthropy.

Lukasz Gacek, 'Confucian Way of Tan Kah Kee: Pursue Excellence, Strive for Perfection', Politeja 5(44), 2016, pp. 172-182 (peer-reviewed article, read in full). Scholarly overview of his work for education, built mainly on C. F. Yong's biography: the reorganisation of his father's indebted firm after 1903, the move from pineapple and rice into rubber manufacturing, shipping-era prosperity, the six Singapore Chinese schools, the Jimei schools from 1913 (normal and secondary schools 1918, further schools to 1920), his pledge of one million dollars for the first two years of Xiamen University and 250,000 dollars a year for twelve years, the 1921 opening with Deng Cuiying and then Lim Boon Keng as presidents, the 1923 Nanyang Siang Pau, his five charity campaigns, his 1929 reorganisation of the Hokkien Huay Kuan, the collapse of his company in February 1934 while he kept supporting the schools, his 1950s redesign and inspection of buildings at Xiamen University and Jimei, and Jamie Mackie's judgement that his aim was not simply to make money. Also covers his politics, which are not scored. The article has slips (for example a 1994 for 1894, a sum in billions of yuan) so only its narrative is used, and it is a secondary retelling of Yong.

Tan Kah Kee Foundation (Singapore), 'Tan Kah Kee: A Biography' timeline (read in full). Foundation-written chronology, so self-interested: after Chop Soon Ann failed in 1903 he started a small pineapple cannery with 7,000 Straits dollars, bought a larger cannery and cleared a 500-acre plantation, set up the Khiam Aik rice mill, planted rubber in 1906 when it was seen as a European business, co-founded Tao Nan School in 1907 with 109 other Hokkien members, founded Jimei School (1913), the Chinese High School (1919) and Xiamen University (1921), moved into shipping (1915) and rubber manufacturing, was Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan president from 1929, saw rubber prices crash and some Xiamen and Jimei building projects stopped, saw Tan Kah Kee Ltd wound up in February 1934 and kept financing schools, and after 1949 rebuilt the Jimei schools. Much of the wording ('foresight', 'bold decision') is promotional.

Xiamen University, 'Founder: Tan Kah Kee (1874-1961)', en.xmu.edu.cn (updated December 2024; read in full). University-written founder profile, so self-interested: built a diversified rubber conglomerate, helped found five Chinese schools in Singapore and gave 30,000 dollars to the Anglo-Chinese School in 1919, set up a normal school in Fujian in 1918 and made sure the new Xiamen University (1921) had a strong education department, campaigned for a decade for a teacher-training school in Singapore that opened in 1941, and wrote his memoirs. Contains an internal slip (he is said to be 17 when starting the cannery in 1904 although born in 1874), and states employment of 10,000 where other sources give 30,000, so no staff numbers are carded.

Xiamen University, 'Blending Cultures and Building Dreams: The Architectural Legacy of Mr. Tan Kah Kee' (feature, 11 June 2024; read in full). University feature on the 'Jiageng' buildings: says he chose the Xiamen site on the old training ground of Zheng Chenggong and laid down principles of economy, practicality, aesthetics and joining immediate needs to long-term vision for the campus, and describes the first group of buildings (the Qunxian complex) and its later 1950s successors. Institutional and promotional; says nothing of how closely he supervised the work.

National Library Board Singapore, 'Of Towchangs and the Republic Beard: Dr Lim Boon Keng's Life and Achievements', BiblioAsia vol. 2 no. 4 (January 2007; read in full). A biographical article about another man that records, from the other side, that in 1921 Lim Boon Keng accepted Tan Kah Kee's invitation to be president of Xiamen University and spent the next sixteen years running it. Used for that single fact; independent of the Tan Kah Kee biographies.

China Daily Xiamen channel (Information Office of the Xiamen Municipal Government), 'Tan Kah Kee' celebrities profile (updated 5 May 2019; read in full). Local-government profile: says he set up Jimei Primary School in 1912, that Xiamen University (1921) was then the only wholly private university in China and that he supported it until the government took it over in 1937, and that by selling his Singapore property and raising donations he funded the expansion of the Jimei schools and Xiamen University with more than 10 million yuan. State-run and promotional, and its dates differ from the foundation's (Jimei 1912 against 1913).

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_tkk_tci1908, src_tkk_roots, src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_gacek | 1903-1923 | contemporary trade directory, heritage story, foundation timeline, scholarly article] After his father's rice firm failed (1903 in the foundation and Gacek, 1904 in the university profile) he started his own pineapple cannery, and a 1908 trade directory independently shows three canneries, a 600-acre plantation and a rubber estate by then; he co-founded Tao Nan School in 1907 with 109 others, founded Jimei School (1913), the Chinese High School (1919) and Xiamen University (1921), and in 1923 started the newspaper Nanyang Siang Pau (Roots, Gacek). The business start is independently confirmed; the school founding comes from one biographical tradition repeated by the foundation, the university and the heritage story. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.6 to 72 / 0.54 because the founding acts are repeated across sources that share one tradition.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_tkk_tci1908, src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_gacek | 1906-1915 | contemporary trade directory, foundation timeline, scholarly article] The 1908 directory independently records a 400-acre estate of one-year-old Para rubber beside his canneries; the foundation says he planted rubber in 1906 when it was seen as a European business and moved into shipping in 1915, and Gacek says the First World War brought him great prosperity. The facts are documented, but 'foresight' is the foundation's word and the sources do not say how he judged these openings. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.44 and reclassified from strong_inference to inference because only the 1908 rubber estate is independent of the promotional timeline.

adaptability.rationale: [src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_roots, src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_tci1908 | 1903-1934 | foundation timeline, heritage story, scholarly article, contemporary trade directory] His business moved from pineapple canning to rice milling, rubber planting, rubber manufacturing and shipping (foundation, Roots), and the foundation says that when pineapple profits fell he deliberately diversified; the 1908 directory shows the first stage of that shift. After the rubber price collapse he cut back his Xiamen and Jimei building (foundation, Gacek), and the company was wound up in 1934. The sequence of businesses is confirmed by several sources; part of the shifting was forced, and the final outcome was a liquidation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.48 because the sources agree on the sequence but the motive for each change is only given by the promotional timeline.

persistence.rationale: [src_tkk_roots, src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_xiamengov | 1903-1950 | heritage story, scholarly article, foundation timeline, local-government profile] Roots says that when his father's businesses failed he worked to shut them down and clear the debts; Gacek and the foundation say that after the 1920s rubber price collapse he cut back Xiamen and Jimei building but that when his company collapsed in February 1934 he kept supporting the schools; the Xiamen government profile says he later funded their expansion with more than 10 million yuan by selling his Singapore property and raising donations. Several episodes, but all of them come from one biographical tradition and the later funding is described by promotional sources. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.52 because the episodes are repeated by sources that share one tradition and the funding totals come from promotional profiles.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_roots, src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_xmufounder | 1907-1954 | scholarly article, heritage story, foundation timeline, university profile] Gacek (via Yong) says he pledged one million dollars for Xiamen University's first two years and 250,000 dollars a year for twelve more, quotes Jamie Mackie's judgement that his primary aim was not simply to make money but to contribute to China's modernisation through education and new industries, and says he went on funding the schools after his firm collapsed; Roots says he reinvented himself to serve communities in Singapore and China and set up more than ten schools; the foundation and university profile list the schools and the 1918 Fujian normal school. The commitment is documented across 1907-1950s, but the strongest quotations come from admiring institutional or scholarly summaries of one biography. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent) and CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.6 to 74 / 0.54 because the supporting sources largely retell Yong and institutional hagiography, and a scholar's characterisation of motive is not independent behaviour. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.54 -> 72@0.5. every substantive source follows one tradition (Yong/NLB); no critical biography read.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_xmuarch | 1919-1921 | scholarly article, university feature] Gacek says that when planning Xiamen University he set aside a million dollars for the first two years and 250,000 dollars a year for the next twelve; the university's feature says he chose the site and set principles of economy, practicality, aesthetics and joining immediate needs to long-term vision. One funding plan from a secondary scholarly summary and one promotional institutional statement. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.48 to 60 / 0.42 and reclassified from strong_inference to inference because the second item is promotional and neither describes his method.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_tkk_roots, src_tkk_gacek | 1920s-1954 | heritage story, scholarly article] Roots says his success was attributed to a fastidious nature and involvement in every stage of the supply chain, and Gacek says that in the 1950s he spent time planning, designing and inspecting the construction of school buildings and that twenty-four Xiamen University buildings completed in 1954 were personally designed by him. Both lines are second-hand characterisations drawn from other writers. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.48 to 60 / 0.4 and reclassified from strong_inference to inference because one line is an attributed adjective and the other a scholar's summary of Yong.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_roots | 1907-1929 | foundation timeline, scholarly article, heritage story] He was among the founders of Tao Nan School in 1907, chaired the 1923-founded Ee Hoe Hean Club for Chinese businessmen, was elected president of the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan in 1929 and reorganised it (Gacek says he held the post until 1949), and chaired the Tientsin Flood Relief Fund of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce in 1917 (Gacek, foundation). Offices held show standing more than desire to lead, and the lists come from one biographical tradition. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.5 to 64 / 0.44 because offices are not the same as the drive to lead and the sources repeat each other.

collaboration.rationale: [src_tkk_biblioasia, src_tkk_gacek, src_tkk_foundation, src_tkk_roots | 1907-1921 | library-board article, scholarly article, foundation timeline, heritage story] He founded Tao Nan School together with 109 other Hokkien community members (foundation, Gacek), put Deng Cuiying and then Lim Boon Keng in charge of Xiamen University, Lim accepting his invitation in 1921 and running it for sixteen years (the NLB article on Lim, an independent source, and Gacek), and mentored Lee Kong Chian and Tan Lark Sye (Roots). The Lim invitation is independently confirmed; how he actually worked with others is not described. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.42 because only one item is independent and none shows working practice.

portrait.source: Halftone portrait numbered 10 and captioned 'Tan Kah Kee' on the plate 'Business Men of Singapore' (twenty numbered portraits, between pages 715 and 716) in Arnold Wright and H. A. Cartwright (eds.), Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya (London: Lloyd's Greater Britain Publishing Company, 1908), the same volume whose entry on p. 712 profiles Tan Kah Kee, rice merchant trading as Kiam Eik; Cornell University Library scan on the Internet Archive (item cu31924023134368, page image n722, 2514 x 3334). The shipped file is the circular frame of portrait 10 cropped from the page image (492 x 492) with the surrounding page content masked to white; no upscaling. The photographer is not named.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: published in London and Singapore in 1908 (before 1931); the photographer is not named, so there is no creator-death basis; the Internet Archive record for the Cornell scan carries no rights statement of its own
portrait.attribution: Unnamed photographer, portrait of Tan Kah Kee in Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya (Lloyd's Greater Britain Publishing Company, 1908); Cornell University Library scan via the Internet Archive (cropped).
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer; reproduced in Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya (London: Lloyd's Greater Britain Publishing Company, 1908)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (lead) / REPLACED after the single bounded retry succeeded. The lead (Commons 'Chenjiageng.JPG', 2005 photograph of a statue, CC BY-SA 3.0) was dropped: it depicts a modern statue, not the man, and carries a share-alike licence. Other routes checked: (a) National Archives of Singapore / Tan Kah Kee Memorial Museum photographs (Commons 'Tan Kah Kee, Lee Kong Chian, and Tan Lark Sye, 1946', the 'young Tan Kah Kee' Lee Brothers Studio portrait c.1910s-1920 and the c.1940 portrait): the NAS record pages return an empty bot-wall response (not bypassed; one attempt with a browser-style request header was blocked and not repeated), and search-result summaries of the NAS records for this collection state that commercial use and reproduction require written permission from the copyright owner, so the holder, not the Commons PD-Singapore tag, governs and the route was not used; (b) Commons PRC-era portraits ('Tan Kah Kee, Zhuang Mingli and Mao Zedong' 1949, the 1949-1960 foundation portrait, the CPPCC 1949 portrait): PD-China only, one explicitly tagged Not-PD-US-URAA, unknown authors, not used; (c) the 1911 photograph with Sun Yat-sen and the 1940 Malayan Comfort Mission photograph (a CC BY-SA permission-ticket scan): group images of uncertain US status and licence, not used. The replacement is a 1908 halftone portrait in Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya (Lloyd's Greater Britain Publishing Company), plate 'Business Men of Singapore': twenty numbered portraits with a printed key; I read the key on the page scan ('10. Tan Kah Kee') and the number 10 printed inside the circular portrait, and the same volume's p. 712 entry profiles Tan Kah Kee, rice merchant trading as Kiam Eik, son of Tan Kee Peck, with three pineapple factories and a young rubber estate, which matches the other sources, so identity rests on caption plus text. Resemblance to later photographs of him was checked by eye only and is not claimed. Rights basis: published in 1908, public domain in the US by age; photographer unnamed; the Internet Archive item (Cornell University Library scan) has no rights statement of its own. KIND likeness (a reproduction of a lifetime photograph). Quality caveat: a small halftone, 492 x 492 pixels, cropped from the 2514 x 3334 page scan, circular frame with the page masked to white, not upscaled. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13) Q709049 label 'Tan Kah Kee', description 'Chinese businessman (1874-1961)', Chinese label 陈嘉庚, instance of human, born 21 October 1874, died 12 August 1961, citizenship Singapore, Malaysia, Republic of China; no Korean label or sitelink. NATIONALITY CN, SG (Wikidata also lists Malaysia; Roots says he held British citizenship until 1957; none of those is coded). REGION south_asia: the 11 controlled ids have no Southeast Asia value, and every Southeast Asian precedent in the repo (lee-kuan-yew SG, jose-rizal PH, kartini ID, ho-chi-minh VN, raden-saleh ID) is coded south_asia. ERA 20th_century. KOREAN NAME 천자겅 is a transliteration of the Mandarin name 陈嘉庚 (Chen Jiageng) under the standard Korean transcription; there is no Wikidata ko label and no Korean Wikipedia article, so this is a choice, not a label. CLASSIFICATION: occupations entrepreneur, philanthropist, educator; fields business, education; tags founder, organizer; archetypes entrepreneurial_builder, institution_builder (precedent: institution_builder used twice before). POLITICS: his wartime relief work, anti-Japanese organising, his stance on the Kuomintang and Communists, the newspapers' political line, his 1949 return to China and his offices in the People's Republic are NOT scored or carded; scoring is limited to his behaviour as builder of enterprises and schools (the canneries and rubber business, Tao Nan, Ai Tong, the Chinese High School, the Jimei schools and Xiamen University). Offices in community bodies are used only lightly under leadership_drive. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Roots.gov.sg heritage story (full); 1908 Twentieth Century Impressions of British Malaya (his entry and the plate); Gacek 2016 in Politeja (full PDF); Tan Kah Kee Foundation timeline (full); Xiamen University founder profile and its Jiageng architecture feature (full); BiblioAsia on Lim Boon Keng (full, one fact); China Daily Xiamen profile (full). Wikipedia not used. Not opened or not readable: the NLB Infopedia article (empty response), the NAS photograph records (bot wall), C. F. Yong's biography (only as retold by Gacek and Roots), Tan's own Nanqiao Huiyilu, the Singapore Memory records, the ThinkChina article, Wang Gungwu's remarks beyond the Roots quote. A small blog copying the NLB blurb and a university Lee Kong Chian page were read and not cited. PERSPECTIVES: government heritage story; contemporary commercial directory; peer-reviewed article; foundation named for him (self-interested); university he founded (self-interested); an independent library-board article on his university's president; a Chinese local-government profile. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: the 1908 directory, Roots and Gacek; the rest are institutional or promotional. All the biography sources lean on one tradition (the NLB biography and Yong), so no row rises above 0.54. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: his father's firm failed in 1903 (foundation, Gacek) or 1904 (Roots, university profile); Jimei Primary School dated 1912 (government profile) or 1913 (foundation, Gacek); employees 10,000 (university) or 30,000 (Roots, Gacek); 'more than ten' (Roots body) or 100 institutions (Roots summary); the university profile says he was 17 in 1904 although born in 1874; Gacek has typographical slips. None of those counts or contested dates is carded except as a range ('around 1903-04', 'early 1910s'). No adversarial or critical biography was read: the critical voices are limited to the rubber collapse and the 1934 winding-up, so the profile is probably more flattering than a full study would be, and the lead should treat all rows as moderate. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS on all six (cards: 1 Xiamen University and the Jimei schools; 2 the business built from the pineapple cannery; 3 the Singapore schools). SELF-CALIBRATION: reviewed persistence, adaptability and impact_motivation (all lowered; impact_motivation also by the concentration check); the concentration check lowered seven rows in all (proactive_agency, opportunity_sensing, impact_motivation, planning_orientation, detail_orientation, leadership_drive, collaboration). Raise flags: none. Sparse by design: nine rows, no conflict_tolerance, persuasiveness, risk_tolerance or achievement_drive rows because the sources do not document them apart from his politics. tan-kah-kee:impact_motivation RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.54 -> 72@0.5. every substantive source follows one tradition (Yong/NLB); no critical biography read.
